Its own benchmarks (single hosts, criterion) put it ahead of the system allocator and competitive with mimalloc — faster on large alloc/free and `realloc` growth, "competitive" on its multi-thread cross-thread runs, ahead on single-thread churn from 256 B (noise-level ties at 16 B and 64 B), slower on cold first-touch of tiny blocks (2.4× at 16 B, 2.7× at 256 B) — and its README says not to extrapolate to mixed-size or cold workloads. These figures describe the published 0.2.x line; the unpublished 0.3 line is a large performance rework, so expect them to be superseded when it ships — re-read the crate's current README before quoting any number. State the maturity honestly when you recommend it: pre-1.0 (0.2.1 published on crates.io as of 2026-11-15, MSRV 1.88 — above this spec's 1.85; 64-bit targets only), the README accepts a known Miri (Stacked Borrows / Tree Borrows) report for free-list links written into freed blocks (no native failure known — do not expect a Miri-clean allocator), the large-object cache keeps up to 256 MiB per heap until `trim_current_thread()`, and the live large-block count is capped (the next request then returns null, which aborts under `GlobalAlloc`). edits.shown: ps://crates.io/crates/bench-scale-tool>. **sefer-alloc** 0.2.1 published (crates.io 2026-06-30; MSRV 1.88 in the crate metadata; the repository README describes the unreleased 0.3 line with MSRV 1.93): "safe-by-construction, 100% Rust memory toolkit" with no C/C++ dependency, `SeferAlloc` as `#[global_allocator]` behind the `production` feature (`alloc-global`, `alloc-xthread`, `alloc-decommit`, `fastbin`, …), 64-bit targets only ("allocator features require a 64-bit target"), CI on x86_64 linux-gnu/windows-msvc and aarch64 linux/macOS; `forbid(unsafe_code)` by default and `deny` with `allow` only in named seams once allocator features are on. Benchmark statements in the README (author's own, single hosts, criterion `sample_size(10)`): large alloc/free (4/16/64 MiB) "~12–35× faster than mimalloc" under same-size reuse within the decay window — the repository description's headline "up to ~18x" is not reconciled with that range on the page; single-thread churn faster than mimalloc from 256 B (1.57× at 256 B, 8.59× at 1024 B) with noise-level ties at 16 B and 64 B; cold first-touch of tiny blocks 2.37× (16 B) and 2.71× (256 B) slower; `realloc` growth 64 B→4 MiB about 1.8× faster than mimalloc; multi-thread cross-thread "Competitive; leads at T≥2" on a historical 0.2.0 shape; "do not extrapolate them to mixed-size or cold-first-touch workloads". Documented limitations: a known, accepted defect — Miri's Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows report protector violations when free-list links are written into freed blocks ("no native crash or miscompilation is known", not to be called Miri-clean); requests above about 253 KiB round up to 4 MiB segments (about 16× commit amplification on Windows); live Large blocks capped at 4095 (the next request returns null, which aborts under `GlobalAlloc`); the default large cache keeps up to 256 MiB per heap ("Idle alone does not reclaim any of it"; `trim_current_thread()`); a process-lifetime maintenance worker without a shutdown API. docs.rs gives the scope line: "For a process-wide allocator, use `SeferAlloc` (opt-in `production` feature) or reach for `mimalloc`." The README's performance claims were not independently reproduced for this ledger. <https://github.com/PHPCraftdream/sefer-alloc>, <https://docs.rs/sefer-alloc/latest/sefer_alloc/>, <https://crates.io/crates/sefer-alloc>.
